cards.def: Lyman Beecher was probably the most celebrated minister of the Republic, a conservative evangelical who sought to restore America to "the moral government of God" through revivals and the Benevolent Empire, while several of his children became more radical reformers.

Charles Grandison Finney was the founder of modern revivalism, a former lawyer who used the "new measures," endorsed free will, and declared that a revival "is not a miracle" but "a purely scientific result of the right use of constituted means."
Richard Allen was a former Delaware slave who bought his freedom and became the first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, organized at Philadelphia.
Dorothea Dix was a Boston Unitarian schoolteacher who took the lead in creating state-supported asylums to treat the mentally ill.
Horace Mann was a Unitarian reformer who strove to give children of poor and working-class families greater access to public schooling.
Ralph Waldo Emerson was a disenchanted Unitarian minister who sparked Transcendentalism, called for a distinctive national literature in "The American Scholar," and advised, "Trust thyself."

Henry David Thoreau lived in relative solitude at Walden Pond to demonstrate self-reliance, wrote that "the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation," and argued in "On Civil Disobedience" that the only obligation was to do what he thought right.
Walt Whitman, author of Leaves of Grass, exalted the emotions, nature, and the individual with a joyous democratic spirit.
Nathaniel Hawthorne, in The Scarlet Letter, and Herman Melville, in Moby-Dick, were darker writers of the American Renaissance who did not share the Transcendentalists' sunny optimism.
John Humphrey Noyes, a revival convert of Charles Finney, announced that he had reached moral perfection and founded the Oneida Community on the doctrine of complex marriage.
Joseph Smith founded Mormonism after announcing that he had been led to golden tablets from which he produced the Book of Mormon, built a large community at Nauvoo, and was murdered.

William Lloyd Garrison was a white Boston editor who launched The Liberator, rejected gradual emancipation and colonization, demanded immediate abolition and racial equality, and later embraced perfectionism and women's rights.
Sarah and Angelina Grimké were southern-born abolitionists whose work led Sarah to write Letters on the Condition of Women, linking the oppression of women to that of slaves.
Frederick Douglass was a leading Black abolitionist, and free African Americans like him were a vital source of support for the movement, including as a majority of The Liberator's subscribers.
Sojourner Truth was a prominent Black abolitionist who, with other free African Americans, was a vital source of support for the antislavery movement.
Harriet Tubman was an escaped slave and famous Underground Railroad conductor who repeatedly returned to the South and eventually escorted more than 200 slaves to freedom.

cards.term: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott
cards.def: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott were abolitionists who, after being forced to sit behind a curtain at a world antislavery convention in London, organized the Seneca Falls conference that launched the women's rights movement.
Harriet Beecher Stowe, a daughter of Lyman Beecher, wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin, the most successful piece of antislavery literature in the nation's history.
